messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan had spent most of his adult life in situations where other people relied on his steadiness, first as a bomb disposal technician and later, in retirement, as the man family and neighbours still described as calm in a crisis. That long history of control made the period after his son’s illness feel even more humiliating to him. At 58, married and living with his wife in the same South Asian community where their children had grown up, Rajan found himself undone by something he could not dismantle, predict, or secure: his child lying critically ill in hospital.

It began when his son was admitted with a life-threatening illness and Rajan sat through long hours in corridors that smelled sharply of antiseptic. The smell stayed with him even after he left the ward, and now it could seize him instantly in a clinic, a pharmacy aisle, or sometimes just at the entrance to a hospital. He would catch that clean, chemical scent and feel as if he had been dropped back into those first days, waiting for news that might change with each doctor’s appearance. The sight of needles, drips, and other medical equipment was just as potent. A nurse adjusting an IV line or a tray of syringes could make him go rigid before he had time to look away, his chest tightening and his body reacting with a force that startled him. He had also found himself increasingly uneasy around children, especially in places where they were running, laughing, or being carried by parents. What should have felt ordinary now had an edge of dread, because children were no longer just children to him; they were reminders of how quickly the safety of family life could be shattered.

At the time of the illness, Rajan had tried to stay useful. He had sat by the bed, watched the monitors, and listened to the staff explain procedures he did not fully understand. But even then he knew there were moments he could not control. His son could deteriorate, alarms could sound, and Rajan could do nothing to prevent it. Since then he had come to believe, with a bleak certainty that embarrassed him, that he was a weak person because his reactions were so strong. He had spent years being the one others turned to, yet now his own mind betrayed him with sudden fear, horror, anger, and guilt. Sometimes he was struck by the conviction that his reactions meant he was going crazy. He would be sitting at home, or standing in line somewhere, and a smell or a glimpse of medical tubing could instantly bring back the full memory without warning. When that happened, the memory did not arrive like an ordinary recollection. It came back as a complete sensory reliving, vivid and enveloping, with the hospital corridor, the harsh light, the antiseptic smell, and the sight of equipment all seeming present at once. He often described the memories as pictures first, as if he were seeing the scene in still frames before it swallowed him whole.

These episodes left him unsettled and watchful. At night he had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert, as though lowering his guard might allow something terrible to happen again. Even after the immediate medical crisis had passed, he could not shake the sense that bad things could come without warning and that he could not stop them. That helplessness sat heavily with him. It made him scan for danger in places where he used to feel at ease and made ordinary family outings more complicated. His wife noticed that he was more hesitant about going to hospitals for his own appointments, and when family gatherings included young children, he often positioned himself at the edge of the room, not wanting to draw attention to the fact that he was trying to manage himself. He disliked what this did to him. The man who once worked with explosives and trusted procedure now felt exposed by a smell, a needle, or a child’s sudden laughter.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become hard to ignore. He was not looking for someone to tell him that the illness never happened; he knew exactly what had happened. What he wanted was some way to understand why his body and mind still reacted as if the danger were immediate, and whether he could sleep without feeling he had to keep watch. More than anything, Rajan feared that these reactions were proof that he was losing his mind, and he hoped that treatment might help him feel like himself again — steady, capable, and no longer at the mercy of memories that arrived unbidden and felt all too real.
